prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I can’t get rid of useful things and nobody wants to pick them up, I keep forgetting where I lay my umbrella. I don’t leave footprints in the snow anymore, we haven’t had a war on domestic soil in so long I wonder if I still got it. Because once I had it. I heard about a boy who once tied a string to his brother, he tied his brother to the ocean and the ocean to the blackbird— from the ground all the birds look like blackbirds from the ground a Stealth Bomber looks like a spaceship. The aliens are coming, they walk through birthday parties and basically go unnoticed. And this is kind of how I go through life, once I heated up a spoon in the microwave the fish have so much mercury in them they spark. I was handed a bayonet from the Civil War and a copper penny corroded with rust. When they take the Statue of Liberty apart to clean her her neck explodes with a million little spiders. Meanwhile in a forest somewhere someone cut open my grandmother’s belly and filled it with bricks something is coming soon I keep a bucket of lambs blood by the front door.

prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The speaker explores anxiety, forgetfulness, loss, and latent violence through a surreal, associative collage of everyday objects, war relics, animals, aliens, and apocalyptic folklore. The imagery reveals ordinary life as haunted by inherited trauma and approaching danger, suggesting that beneath apparent peace lies persistent dread and a futile desire for protection.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Because, Stealth, Bomber

outputs.L1:
I can’t bring myself to get rid of useful things, and no one wants to pick them up. I keep forgetting where I set down my umbrella. I no longer leave footprints in the snow. We haven’t had a war on domestic soil in so long that I wonder whether I still have it in me—because once, I did.

I heard about a boy who tied a string to his brother; he tied his brother to the ocean, and the ocean to the blackbird. From the ground, all birds look like blackbirds. From the ground, a Stealth Bomber looks like a spaceship.

The aliens are coming. They walk through birthday parties and go essentially unnoticed. This is, in a way, how I move through life. Once, I heated a spoon in the microwave. The fish have so much mercury in them that they spark.

I was handed a bayonet from the Civil War and a copper penny corroded with rust. When they take the Statue of Liberty apart to clean her, her neck explodes with a million tiny spiders.

Meanwhile, in a forest somewhere, someone cut open my grandmother’s belly and filled it with bricks. Something is coming soon. I keep a bucket of lamb’s blood by the front door.
outputs.L2:
I hold on to things that still have value because no one will come collect them, yet I’m always misplacing my umbrella. My tracks no longer mark the snow. It has been such a long time since war reached our own soil that I question whether I still possess what I once did—because there was a time when I had it.  

I once heard of a boy who fastened a cord to his brother, joined his brother to the sea, and linked the sea to a blackbird. Seen from below, every bird appears black; from that same viewpoint, a Stealth Bomber resembles a spacecraft. Extraterrestrials are on their way. They pass through birthday celebrations almost entirely unnoticed. That is more or less how I move through the world.  

One time I put a spoon in the microwave to warm it. Fish contain so much mercury that they give off sparks. Someone placed in my hands a Civil War bayonet and a copper cent eaten away by rust. Whenever the Statue of Liberty is dismantled for cleaning, a million tiny spiders burst from her neck. Elsewhere, deep in some forest, a person sliced open my grandmother’s stomach and packed it with bricks. Something will arrive soon, so I keep a pail of lamb’s blood beside the front entrance.
outputs.L3:
The speaker moves through a world shaped by loss, anxiety, and a persistent inability to let go. They struggle to discard possessions that might still be useful, even as they repeatedly misplace ordinary objects needed in daily life. This tension between hoarding and forgetting creates a sense of instability: familiar things are preserved without clear purpose, while necessary items vanish at the moment they are needed.

That unease extends beyond the domestic sphere. Images of war, weapons, and stealth aircraft evoke violence that has been forgotten, concealed, or left unresolved. At the same time, ordinary reality dissolves into surreal associations linking people, oceans, birds, aliens, and contaminated fish. These strange connections suggest a world in which natural, human, and extraterrestrial life are all vulnerable to the same spreading corruption.

Historical symbols offer no comfort. Objects such as a Civil War bayonet and the Statue of Liberty become disturbing reminders of decay and hidden horror rather than reassuring emblems of courage or freedom. As the imagery grows more ominous, the speaker becomes convinced that an unnamed threat is approaching. In response, they place a bucket of lamb’s blood by the door—a ritualistic gesture of protection that recalls ancient acts of deliverance while underscoring the depth of their fear.
outputs.L4:
The speaker moves through a surreal, associative landscape shaped by anxiety, forgetfulness, loss, and the threat of violence. Everyday objects appear alongside war relics, animals, aliens, and fragments of apocalyptic folklore, creating a collage in which the familiar continually slips into the uncanny. Domestic details offer no lasting comfort: each object seems capable of carrying a buried memory, while each moment of distraction or forgetting hints at something painful that cannot be fully recovered. The speaker’s thoughts do not follow a stable narrative but proceed through abrupt connections, suggesting a mind attempting to organize experiences that remain fragmented by fear and grief.

Within this unstable world, historical violence persists in disguised or displaced forms. Remnants of war intrude upon ordinary life, implying that trauma can be inherited even by those who did not directly experience its original events. Animals and extraterrestrial figures further blur the boundary between genuine danger and imagined threat, while apocalyptic legends give private anxiety a larger, almost mythic scale. These images may seem absurd or fantastical, but they express a serious conviction that catastrophe is always approaching, whether from the past, from beyond the known world, or from within human beings themselves.

As a result, apparent peace becomes deeply unreliable. The speaker searches for shelter, reassurance, or some object capable of providing protection, yet every defense seems temporary or symbolic. Beneath the surface of ordinary existence lies a persistent dread: the fear that violence has not disappeared but is merely dormant, waiting to return. The speaker’s desire for safety is therefore both urgent and futile. No barrier can fully separate the present from inherited trauma, and no charm, memory, or explanation can guarantee protection from future disaster. The surreal imagery ultimately reveals a world in which daily life is haunted by what has already been lost and overshadowed by what may still be coming.
outputs.L5: The stealth bomber moved silently across the night sky, nearly invisible to radar. It was designed to enter heavily defended airspace without detection. Because its shape and special coating absorb radar signals, enemy systems often fail to notice it until the mission is already complete. Combining advanced technology, precision, and secrecy, the stealth bomber remains one of the most powerful aircraft in modern aviation.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem in the voice of an anxious, absentminded speaker, weaving together war, aliens, family folklore, household objects, environmental contamination, and biblical imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
Every morning I misplace the war. I know I left it somewhere near the sugar bowl, beneath the unpaid electric bill, but when I reach for it my hand returns dusted with ash and a little green pollen the government says is harmless. The radio counts backward in a language my teeth almost remember. Perhaps it is the aliens again, tapping their teaspoons against the moon. Perhaps it is only the pipes.

My grandmother used to say our family descended from a woman who married a thunderstorm. Or was swallowed by one. I forget. In every version, she came home carrying a blue child and a jar of rain that never went bad. We kept the jar under the sink beside the bleach, the mouse poison, and six batteries of uncertain purpose. Last winter it began to glow. Father called it inheritance. Mother called it leakage. I wrote DO NOT DRINK on the lid, then drank from the wrong glass.

Outside, the soldiers kneel in the vegetable garden, mistaking cabbages for helmets. Their uniforms are embroidered with tiny planets. One asks whether I have seen his brother, who was taken up in a silver wheel above the refinery. I tell him everyone’s brother has been taken up by something: debt, fever, marriage, heaven. I offer him a dish towel. He wraps it around his wound, and the red roosters printed on the cloth begin crowing.

I should call someone. I keep forgetting whom.

The river arrives at the door wearing a film of gasoline. It smells like rainbows and dead batteries. Two-headed minnows flicker in its pockets. Behind it comes a procession of frogs, each with a small human eye, and behind them an angel in a respirator, dragging seven seals through the mud. The angel asks for Noah. I explain that Noah moved years ago and left no forwarding address. The angel sighs into the filter. Even the Apocalypse, it seems, has paperwork.

In the cupboard, the plates whisper evacuation routes. The toaster dreams of missiles. A spoon bends toward the north whenever the sirens begin. I place my ear against the refrigerator and hear the mothership humming among the leftovers: one bowl of soup, half an onion, the ancient lamb my mother insists is still good.

At supper we set an extra place for the missing. Grandmother, the soldier’s brother, the bees, the clean water, Elijah, whoever forgot us here. My father says grace in the old family way: Lord, protect us from the sky and from what we have poured into the ground. My mother corrects him—it was protect us from the ground and what we have invited from the sky. They argue gently while locusts tap at the windows, wearing the faces of our childhood pets.

I try to remember whether this has happened before.

Somewhere a trumpet sounds. Or a kettle. I rise too quickly and knock over the salt, which spreads across the table like a white, uninhabitable country. Everyone goes quiet. Above the roof, enormous lights turn slowly, searching the dark as if they have lost their keys.

I know exactly how they feel.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a single-paragraph experimental monologue that moves through dreamlike free association. Include an umbrella, footprints in snow, a Stealth Bomber, mercury-filled fish, the Statue of Liberty, and a bucket of lamb’s blood.
counterfactuals.output: I opened the umbrella indoors and a weather of black feathers fell upward, each one whispering the name of a city I had never visited, while footprints in snow crossed the kitchen floor and disappeared beneath the refrigerator, where a Stealth Bomber slept like a folded moth, dreaming in coordinates; when I touched its wing, the sink filled with mercury-filled fish, silver and trembling, their mouths opening onto tiny moons, and the Statue of Liberty leaned through the window to ask whether I had seen her missing shadow, but all I could offer was a bucket of lamb’s blood, warm as an unfinished sentence, which she lifted like a lantern as we followed the footprints into the white distance, the umbrella blooming above us, upside down, catching stars.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a prose poem about the feeling that something terrible is coming, using absurd humor, apocalyptic imagery, strange historical artifacts, and unsettling childhood-story logic?
counterfactuals.output:
By noon, the sky had developed a small but undeniable crack, and through it someone was pouring black salt. The mayor advised us to remain calm and handed out commemorative spoons from the reign of a king who had been dead for eight hundred years and was, according to the spoons, still very disappointed in us.

At school, the children were taught the new emergency alphabet: A is for Ashes, B is for Bell, C is for the Cart That Comes When No One Has Called It. If you reached Z without crying, you were given a sugar mouse and told not to eat its eyes. Naturally, we ate the eyes first. This is how childhood works: the wolf says not to open the blue door, the grandmother says wolves cannot speak, the blue door begins politely coughing.

All afternoon, extinct birds landed on the telephone wires. They carried tiny flags from vanished empires—Byzantium, Atlantis, the Republic of Tuesday. In the museum, Napoleon’s left sock filled with seawater. A curator climbed inside the sarcophagus of a minor pharaoh and refused to come out until history apologized. History, busy sharpening its teeth, did not reply.

We tried ordinary things. We washed the dishes. We paid the gas bill. We moved the armchair away from the window so the window would not get ideas. But the moon rose at four o’clock wearing the red bonnet from the story, and behind it came the wolf, enormous now, with cities stuck between its teeth like parsley.

Still, supper had to be served. The carrots screamed only briefly. Father said the thunder was just furniture being moved in heaven, though everyone knew heaven had been unfurnished since the war. Mother counted us twice and found an extra child beneath the table. It had antlers, a wedding ring, and the sad eyes of a saint whose relics had been misplaced during the Crusades.

“May I stay?” it asked.

“No,” we said, because that is what people say in stories just before the knocking begins.

Then the knocking began—not at the door, but under the earth, slow and mannerly, as if the end of the world had wiped its shoes and brought a cake.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a fragmented, stream-of-consciousness piece in which mundane confessions gradually become uncanny and ominous. Avoid explaining the connections between images, use minimal punctuation, and end with a ritualistic image at a front door.
counterfactuals.output:
I leave cups beside the bed until the water tastes of dust

sometimes I wear the same shirt two days  
sometimes three

I tell people I missed their message  
I watched it arrive  
a small blue light breathing in my hand

there are spoons in the wrong drawer  
receipts in every pocket  
one pale hair wound around the soap

I do not remember buying pears

each morning one is gone

the clock above the sink loses seven minutes whenever I look away  
the neighbor says it has always done that  
the neighbor moved out in February

I still hear his key testing the walls

last night I counted the stairs  
twelve going up  
thirteen coming down

under my pillow a little grit  
black salt perhaps  
perhaps soil from the garden I do not have

I have begun apologizing to empty rooms

not aloud

the mirror clouds before the shower runs  
someone draws a circle there  
then another inside it  
then a door too narrow for shoulders

today every cup beside the bed was full

the water warm

at dusk I found my shoes facing the hallway  
their laces tied together  
their tongues pressed flat as if instructed

outside no cars  
no wind  
only the porch light blinking in groups of four

and at the front door

a bowl of milk  
three bent nails  
my house key standing upright in a mound of ash

around it the wet prints of bare feet

all pointing in
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an eerie contemporary poem blending domestic clutter with American mythology and violence: Civil War relics, stealth aircraft mistaken for spaceships, unnoticed aliens at birthday parties, spiders inside the Statue of Liberty, and a grandmother from a dark fairy tale.
counterfactuals.output:
### **Inventory of the Republic**

In the junk drawer: batteries, birthday candles,  
a minie ball Granddad dug from a field  
where boys once folded into the grass  
under two different flags.

The television whispers weather.  
Above the cul-de-sac, a stealth bomber  
slides through the clouds—black, triangular, silent.  
Everyone runs outside shouting *spaceship*  
except the aliens, who remain at the party,  
eating sheet cake with their delicate hands,  
wearing paper hats, smiling for photographs  
no one will examine closely.

In the laundry room, a jar of buttons  
rattles by itself. The vacuum holds  
three dead moths and a little gray history.  
We keep the saber over the mantel  
though its edge remembers more than we do.

At night, spiders move through Liberty’s copper body,  
stringing their republic from rib to rib.  
They nest in the torch, descend the raised arm,  
drink rain from the green folds of her gown.  
Ships pass below. No one looks up.

Grandmother lives at the tree line  
in a house that smells of apples and iron.  
Her teeth are too white. Her oven is warm.  
She calls us by names our mothers never gave us  
and combs burrs from our hair  
with the tiny bones of soldiers.

By morning, the gift wrap has filled the hallway.  
Plastic soldiers lie facedown beneath the couch.  
A balloon drifts against the ceiling  
like a captured moon.

Outside, the bomber vanishes westward.  
Inside, someone turns off the porch light.

In the dark, the aliens applaud softly.  
In the harbor, the statue scratches.  
Grandmother opens her door  
and the whole country goes in.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
